title: “THERE IS NO FEAR IN LOVE” — THEN WHY ARE YOU STILL TERRIFIED WHEN YOU BELIEVE IN JESUS?
paragraphs: “THERE IS NO FEAR IN LOVE” — THEN WHY ARE YOU STILL TERRIFIED WHEN YOU BELIEVE IN JESUS?

You pray. You believe. You love God. But some nights, your heart still races, your mind imagines the worst, and fear whispers louder than your faith. Does that mean your love for God is incomplete? Or have we misunderstood one of the most beautiful promises in Scripture?
There is a kind of fear that visits people who genuinely love Jesus.
It doesn't always arrive with a scream.
Sometimes it arrives at 2:17 in the morning.

You wake up, stare at the ceiling, and suddenly remember the unpaid bills. The medical results you haven't received. The child who has stopped listening. The marriage that feels increasingly fragile. The mistake you made years ago that still makes you wonder whether God looks at you differently.
You reach for your phone.
You scroll because silence feels unbearable.
You whisper a prayer because you don't know what else to do.
And somewhere between the trembling and the tears, a Bible verse comes back to you.
“There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear.” — 1 John 4:18 (KJV)
And instead of comforting you, it almost breaks you.
Because you are afraid.
Very afraid.
And now you're wondering whether your fear is evidence that something is wrong with your faith.
Maybe you've heard someone say, “If you really trusted God, you wouldn't be afraid.”
Maybe someone told you anxiety is always a sign of weak faith.
Maybe you've smiled in church, lifted your hands during worship, and said, “God is good,” while secretly fighting thoughts you were too ashamed to admit.
You love Jesus.
But you're still scared.
And the question you haven't dared to ask out loud is this:
“Lord, if Your love is supposed to cast out fear, why is fear still living inside me?”
Please don't walk away from this question.
Because the answer is not that Jesus has rejected you.
The answer is hidden in what the apostle John was actually saying.
And when you understand it, you may discover that the verse you've been using to condemn yourself was written to help you become confident in the love of God.
John writes:
Now listen carefully to the original Greek.
“φόβος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ, ἀλλ᾽ ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη ἔξω βάλλει τὸν φόβον.”
Phobos ouk estin en tē agapē, all’ hē teleia agapē exō ballei ton phobon.
A close translation is:
“There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts fear outside.”
The word φόβος (phobos) means fear, dread, or alarm. But its meaning here must be understood from the surrounding verses.
The word τελεία (teleia) comes from teleios, conveying what is complete, mature, or brought to its intended goal.
And βάλλει (ballei) means to throw or cast.
John is describing love that drives fear out.
But what kind of fear?
And whose love is doing the casting?
This is where many well-meaning Christians accidentally turn a promise of assurance into a weapon of shame.
Go back one verse.
“Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment.” — 1 John 4:17 (KJV)
There it is.
The day of judgment.
John is not teaching that a Christian will never be startled, grieve, tremble before surgery, feel afraid during persecution, or struggle with anxious thoughts.
He is speaking particularly about the fear of punishment before God.
The Greek word translated “torment” in the King James Version is κόλασις (kolasis), which means punishment or penalty.
The context makes the meaning unmistakable.
John is addressing the terrifying possibility of standing before a holy God and facing condemnation.
And he is telling believers that God's love, brought to its intended maturity in them, produces confidence rather than the dread of punishment.
Why?
Because salvation does not rest on the emotional steadiness of the person being saved.
It rests on Jesus Christ.
John has already explained the foundation:
“Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” — 1 John 4:10 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not that we loved God.
But that He loved us.
The Gospel does not begin with your ability to love God perfectly.
It begins with God's love demonstrated in sending His Son.
That changes everything.

Because if your assurance depended on never feeling afraid, your salvation would rise and fall with your nervous system, your circumstances, your sleep, your health, and your ability to control every frightening thought.
But the cross of Jesus Christ is not that fragile.
You may wake up shaking.
Christ has not stopped being Savior.
You may cry while praying.
His resurrection has not been undone.
You may struggle to believe tomorrow will be better.
The blood Jesus shed for sinners has not lost its power.
And you may be fighting fear while still genuinely trusting the One who promises never to abandon His people.
Think about the disciples.
They had watched Jesus heal the sick.
They had witnessed His authority.
They had heard His teaching.
And then one night, a storm threatened their boat.
The wind roared. The waves rose. Water entered the vessel.
Experienced fishermen became terrified men.
And Jesus was asleep.
Can you imagine their confusion?
The One who had performed miracles was resting while they believed they were about to die.
They woke Him and cried:
“Lord, save us: we perish.” — Matthew 8:25 (KJV)
They were afraid.
And they called on Jesus.
Notice something beautiful.
Their fear did not prevent them from turning toward Him.
Jesus answered:
“Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?” — Matthew 8:26 (KJV)
He confronted their fear and exposed their little faith.
Scripture does not pretend their response was spiritually mature.
But neither does the story end with Jesus abandoning them because they were frightened.
He arose and rebuked the winds and the sea.
And there was a great calm.
The same disciples who feared the storm were left marveling at the authority of Christ.
Their fear revealed how much they still needed to learn about the One who was with them.
And perhaps that is where you are.
Not faithless.
Not spiritually finished.
But still learning who Jesus is.
Still discovering that the presence of danger does not mean the absence of God.
Still learning that the Lord who commands the sea is worthy of trust even before the wind becomes quiet.
And then there is Peter.
Bold Peter.
The man who declared loyalty so confidently.
The man who said he was ready to die with Jesus.
But when pressure came, Peter denied knowing Him.
Three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The realization.
The eyes of the Savior.
And the crushing knowledge that Peter had done exactly what he promised he would never do.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.” — Luke 22:62 (KJV)
Fear had contributed to his collapse.
His courage failed.
His promise failed.
His confidence in himself failed.
But the story of Peter did not end beside that fire.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ asked Peter three times whether he loved Him.
And Jesus entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
What grace.
The man who denied Jesus was not beyond restoration.
His failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
And Christ's mercy was greater than the scandal of his denial.
This does not mean sin is harmless.
It means the Savior is merciful.
It means that the person who has failed terribly can still find forgiveness and restoration in Jesus Christ.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that.
Because you are not only afraid of tomorrow.
You are afraid of yesterday.
You are afraid that the things you did when nobody was watching have permanently disqualified you from being loved by God.
You remember the lie.
The betrayal.
The secret compromise.
The addiction you promised to leave.
The angry words.
The years of spiritual indifference.
The time you knew what was right and deliberately chose what was wrong.
You have asked God to forgive you, but sometimes you still feel as though heaven is waiting to punish you.
That is why the distinction in 1 John matters so much.
There is a difference between the reverent fear of the Lord and the terror of condemnation.
The Bible does not command us to abandon reverence.
Proverbs 9:10 declares:
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.”
The Hebrew expression is יִרְאַת יְהוָה (yir’at YHWH), the fear of the LORD.
In this wisdom context, it describes reverent recognition of God's holiness, authority, and majesty—a reverence that shapes obedience.
This is not the same as the punishment-centered fear John says mature love casts out.
A child who loves a good father can deeply respect his authority without living in constant terror that every mistake will result in rejection.
In an infinitely greater way, those who belong to Christ are called to approach God with reverence and confidence grounded in His grace.
We must never confuse freedom from condemnation with freedom to sin.
Grace does not make holiness irrelevant.
Grace teaches us to turn away from sin and live for the God who redeemed us.
And repentance is not the price we pay to purchase God's love.
It is part of the response of a heart being turned toward Him.
Now consider another scene.
Not a boat in a storm.
Not a courtyard where Peter denied Jesus.
A garden.
Gethsemane.
The night before the crucifixion.
Jesus knew what was approaching.
Betrayal.
Abandonment.
Mockery.
The cross.
And the Gospel writers do not describe Him as emotionally untouched by the horror ahead.
Mark 14:33 says He began to be deeply distressed and troubled.
Jesus Himself declared:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death.” — Mark 14:34 (KJV)
Luke records His anguish as He prayed.
Yet Jesus remained perfectly obedient to the Father.
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42 (KJV)
We must be careful here.
Jesus' holy anguish cannot simply be equated with every form of human anxiety. His suffering was unique, and His sinless obedience was perfect.
But Gethsemane destroys the careless assumption that profound emotional distress automatically means spiritual failure.
The sinless Son of God experienced genuine human sorrow and anguish without sinning.
And Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our High Priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
So when you approach Jesus trembling, you are not approaching a Savior who is ignorant of suffering.
You are approaching the One who entered human suffering and remained faithful.
The One who understands.
The One who intercedes.
The One who carried our sins to the cross.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a comforting sentence.
It becomes your only lasting hope.
Because the deepest problem in our lives is not merely that we feel afraid.
It is that we are sinners who need reconciliation with a holy God.
No amount of positive thinking can remove guilt before God.
No amount of self-improvement can undo sin.
No religious performance can make us our own saviors.
But Jesus Christ lived in perfect obedience, died for sins, and rose again.
The apostle Paul writes:
No condemnation.
Not because sin never mattered.
But because Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
The Greek word κατάκριμα (katakrima) means condemnation or an adverse judicial sentence.
For those who are in Christ, the verdict of condemnation has been removed.
This is not a blanket declaration that everyone is automatically saved regardless of their relationship to Jesus.
It is a glorious promise for those who belong to Him.
And the invitation of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Christ.
Not to pretend you are innocent.
Not to hide your sins behind religious language.
Not to earn acceptance through impressive spirituality.
But to come to the crucified and risen Savior in faith.
To stop defending what God calls sin.
To confess.
To turn.
To trust Him.
And to receive the grace you could never deserve.
Maybe that is the real battle taking place in your heart.
You have spent so long trying to prove you are a good Christian that you have forgotten the Christian life begins with admitting you need a Savior.
You are exhausted from pretending.
Exhausted from being the strong one.
Exhausted from telling everyone, “I'm blessed,” when you barely made it through the night.
You know the language of faith.
But you're afraid to admit the depth of your struggle.
Listen.
There is a difference between surrendering to fear as your master and admitting that fear is a struggle you need God's help to face.
The Psalms give us language for this.
David wrote:
“What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.” — Psalm 56:3 (KJV)
Not “I have never been afraid.”
Not “I will only trust You once all fear disappears.”
But “When I am afraid, I will trust.”
The Hebrew is striking:
יוֹם אִירָא אֲנִי אֵלֶיךָ אֶבְטָח
Yom ira, ani elekha evtach.
A close rendering is:
“When I am afraid, I will trust in You.”
Fear is acknowledged.
Trust is chosen.
And the trust is directed toward God.
That is not an excuse to nurture unbelief.
It is an invitation to bring our weakness into the presence of the Lord rather than hiding it.
Faith does not require you to lie about your circumstances.
Faith calls you to tell the truth about God in the middle of them.
You may be afraid of losing your job and still trust the Lord to provide.
You may be afraid of a diagnosis and still believe that Christ holds your life.
You may be afraid of grief, rejection, or the unknown and still choose obedience.
You may need pastoral counsel, Christian community, and professional care for persistent anxiety while continuing to walk faithfully with Jesus.
Seeking appropriate help is not automatically a rejection of God's power.
And experiencing symptoms of anxiety is not, by itself, proof that you are living in sin.
Our bodies are vulnerable.
Our minds can become overwhelmed.
Trauma, illness, exhaustion, and prolonged stress can affect how fear is experienced.
The Bible does not authorize us to condemn every frightened believer as spiritually defective.
At the same time, Scripture does call us to grow in trust, bring our concerns to God, and resist allowing fear to govern our obedience.
Paul writes in Philippians 4:6–7 about bringing our requests to God through prayer and thanksgiving, and about the peace of God guarding our hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.
That peace is not a promise that every difficult circumstance will immediately disappear.
It is the peace of belonging to God and depending on Him in the midst of circumstances we cannot control.
Sometimes God calms the storm.
Sometimes He sustains His people through it.
Sometimes the answer comes quickly.
Sometimes endurance is learned over a long and painful season.
But His love is not measured by how quickly your circumstances become comfortable.
It was demonstrated decisively at Calvary.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8 (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Before we could clean ourselves up.
Before we could offer an impressive record of obedience.
Before we could present ourselves as people who deserved His favor.
Christ died for us.
This is why the perfect love of 1 John 4 cannot be reduced to a command to manufacture perfect emotions.
John says:
“We love him, because he first loved us.” — 1 John 4:19 (KJV)
God's initiating love is the foundation.
Our love is the response.
And as His love reaches its intended maturity in us, fear of final punishment gives way to confidence in Christ.
That is a lifelong journey of growth, not a test requiring you to become emotionally invulnerable overnight.
And now I want to speak to the person who almost stopped reading because this feels painfully personal.
The person who has been asking God for a sign.
The mother who lies awake worrying about her children.
The father who feels ashamed because he cannot provide everything his family needs.
The young believer who keeps falling into temptation and wonders whether repentance is still possible.
The Christian who sits in church while quietly battling panic.
The person who is afraid of dying.
The one who wonders whether God is angry every time something goes wrong.
You do not need another performance.
You need the truth.
And the truth is that God's holiness is real, sin is serious, judgment is certain, and Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Do not use God's love as permission to remain in rebellion.
But do not use your remaining fears as evidence that Christ is unwilling to receive those who come to Him.
Hear His words:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
What a promise.
Not because we deserve it.
But because He is gracious.
You can come with your guilt.
Come with your trembling.
Come with your confession.
Come with the faith that feels small.
Come ready to surrender the sin you have been defending.
Come believing that the Savior who died and rose again is worthy of your trust.
And if you have already come to Christ, stop treating every frightened moment as a fresh verdict against your salvation.
Look to Him.
Not to the strength of your emotional response.
Not to the absence of every anxious thought.
Not to how impressive your faith appears to other people.
Look to Jesus.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His promises.
His ongoing intercession for His people.
And when fear returns, remember Psalm 56:3.
“When I am afraid, I will trust in thee.”
Maybe you'll need to pray that verse more than once.
Maybe you'll need to repeat it through tears.
Maybe you'll need a brother or sister in Christ to sit beside you while you struggle to believe it.
That is not a reason to disappear from the fellowship of believers.
It is a reason to seek encouragement, prayer, biblical counsel, and the help you need.
And perhaps someone reading your words today is carrying the same secret burden.
You do not have to disclose private details or explain everything that has happened.
A few honest words may become the beginning of a meaningful conversation and an opportunity for others to pray with you.
And if this message has exposed an area where fear has led you away from obedience, don't merely admire the words.
Respond to God.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask Him to teach you to trust Him more deeply.
Because the goal of this article is not to make you feel inspired for five minutes.
It is to point you toward a lifetime of following Jesus Christ.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn spiritual struggles into entertainment.
But to keep directing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, biblical discipleship, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
There are people scrolling Facebook tonight who will never enter a church building unless someone first reaches them with the truth of Christ.
There are wounded believers who need encouragement.
There are seekers who have questions they are afraid to ask.
There are Christians who have grown spiritually cold and need to hear the call to return to Jesus.
And sometimes a simple act of sharing can place a message of biblical hope in front of someone who desperately needs it.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
Not because an algorithm determines your faithfulness.
But because the Gospel is worth making known.
Send this privately to someone who has been quietly struggling.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has drifted, and the person who has never understood the Gospel to follow along.
One message will never replace the patient work of discipleship, but it can become a doorway into a deeper conversation about Jesus.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this ministry, I want to invite you into something more personal.
But let us be biblically clear.
Scripture teaches generosity and faithful stewardship. Believers should not neglect the responsibilities of supporting their local church, caring for their families, and helping those in need.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving is to be purposeful, willing, and not under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not because you fear God will love you less if you don't.
But because you want to help more people encounter biblical truth.
Those products can be useful reminders, gifts, and resources, but they are not the heart of this mission.
Jesus is.
The Word of God is.
The Gospel is.
And the opportunity to help people grow as disciples of Christ is far more important than anything we could sell.
God's love is not merchandise.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is not a membership benefit.
Now return with me, just for a moment, to that room at 2:17 in the morning.
The ceiling has not changed.
The bills may still be waiting.
The diagnosis may still be unknown.
The child may still be far from home.
The marriage may still need difficult conversations and genuine healing.
The storm outside may not have stopped.
But something inside your understanding of God can change.
You no longer have to read “There is no fear in love” as though John were saying, “If you ever feel afraid, you do not belong to Jesus.”
You can read it in the light of the cross.
The love of God revealed in Christ is powerful enough to deliver those who belong to Him from the dread of final condemnation.
And as you grow in that love, you can learn to approach God with increasing confidence.
Not because you are perfect.
Because Jesus is the perfect Savior.
Not because your heart never trembles.
Because your hope rests in the One who conquered sin and death.
Not because you know what tomorrow holds.
Because you know the One to whom you have entrusted your life.
So tonight, if you are afraid, pray.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you are weary, seek help and encouragement.
If you are uncertain of your standing before God, turn to Christ and trust His Gospel.
And if you belong to Jesus, remember that your assurance is not found in proving you can never feel fear again.
It is found in the crucified and risen Lord.
You do not have to pretend the storm is harmless.
You do not have to pretend the tears are not real.
You do not have to pretend you are stronger than you are.
You are invited to trust the Savior who is stronger than you could ever be.
The miracle is not that your hands never tremble again. It is that even with trembling hands, you can reach for the Savior whose hands were pierced for you.
